## In 60 seconds

A **voltage map** colors each site by the **peak-to-peak amplitude** of its electrogram. Low amplitude is read as
diseased tissue or scar, but the amplitude also depends on the recording. In the m03 model, the unipolar amplitude is
$A/a$, so it falls as the electrode lifts off. A closely spaced bipole records $\tfrac98 A d\lvert\cos\theta\rvert/a^2$,
so it falls faster with height and also depends on the angle between the bipole and the wavefront. If wavefront
directions are random, healthy tissue reads below a third of its aligned amplitude about one time in five. The larger
of two orthogonal bipoles never drops below $1/\sqrt2$ of it, and the largest projection of the pair is nearly
independent of direction at small spacing. Noise sets a floor: with no signal, the peak-to-peak of 100 noise samples
is about five noise SDs. Cutoffs such as 0.5 mV and 1.5 mV then trade sensitivity for specificity, and contact moves
healthy tissue toward them.

## From the field

- **The classic ventricular cutoffs.** In an early study of 16 patients, normal ventricular endocardium was defined
  as bipolar amplitude above 1.5 mV, from sinus-rhythm maps of 6 patients without structural heart disease, and dense
  scar as below 0.5 mV [@marchlinski2000].
- **Atrial normal values depend little on electrode size, scar maps more.** In 10 patients with normal atria, the
  fifth percentile of bipolar voltage was 0.48 mV with 3.5-mm electrodes and 0.52 mV with 1-mm electrodes. In 20
  patients with scar, the area below 0.5 mV was 20.4 cm² with the larger electrodes and 14.7 cm² with the smaller
  ones [@anter2015].
- **Contact force and direction matter.** In 14 patients with repaired tetralogy of Fallot, contact force correlated
  with unipolar and bipolar voltage [@teijeira2018]. In 10 swine, bipolar voltage from a stationary array differed by
  32% (13–53%) between orthogonal activation directions, but by 11% (5–18%) when the catheter roved [@yavin2021].

## Derivations

**Symbols used throughout.** $U$ unipolar potential with strength $A$; $s$ front distance; $a = w + h$ front width
plus electrode height (m03); $\operatorname{pp}$ peak-to-peak; $d$ bipole spacing; $\theta$ angle between bipole and
propagation; $q$ a fraction of the aligned amplitude; $n$ number of independent noise samples; $\sigma$ noise SD;
$\phi$, $\Phi$ standard normal density and distribution; $t$ a voltage cutoff; $m_s$, $m_n$ median voltages of scar and
healthy tissue; $\sigma_s$, $\sigma_n$ SDs of their logarithms.

### Amplitude

From the m03 front, $U = As/(s^2 + a^2)$ peaks at $s = \pm a$, and $dU/ds$ ranges from $A/a^2$ to $-A/(8a^2)$:

$$
\operatorname{pp}(U) = \frac{A}{a}, \qquad \operatorname{pp}(B) \to \frac98\,\frac{A\,d\lvert\cos\theta\rvert}{a^2} \;\; (d\lvert\cos\theta\rvert \ll a), \qquad \operatorname{pp}(B) \to \frac{A}{a} \;\; (d\lvert\cos\theta\rvert \gg a)
$$ {#eq-m23-amplitude}

A close bipole is a directional derivative (m03, [eq-m03-bipolar-gradient](m03-electrograms.qmd#eq-m03-bipolar-gradient)),
so its amplitude falls as $1/a^2$, faster than the unipolar $1/a$. Lifting the electrode from 1 to 2 mm kept 0.57 of
the unipolar amplitude, 0.42 of a 2-mm bipole's and 0.32 of a 0.2-mm bipole's (lab part A). For a 2-mm bipole at 1 mm
height, the small-spacing formula overstates the amplitude by half, so use the exact form there.

**Key takeaways**

- Bipolar voltage reflects contact more strongly than unipolar.
- Cutoffs belong to a catheter: spacing and electrode size change the reading.

### Direction

In the small-spacing limit a bipole reads $\lvert\cos\theta\rvert$ times its aligned amplitude. For uniformly random
in-plane directions:

$$
P\bigl(\lvert\cos\theta\rvert < q\bigr) = \frac{2}{\pi}\arcsin q, \qquad \mathrm E\lvert\cos\theta\rvert = \frac2\pi, \qquad \max\bigl(\lvert\cos\theta\rvert, \lvert\sin\theta\rvert\bigr) \ge \frac{1}{\sqrt2}
$$ {#eq-m23-direction}

With $q = 1/3$, the ratio of the 0.5-mV and 1.5-mV cutoffs, healthy tissue exactly at the normal cutoff reads as dense
scar 21.6% of the time. In the lab, a 2-mm bipole did so 14% of the time; finite spacing softens the cosine. The larger
of two orthogonal bipoles never fell below the cutoff. The largest projection of the pair, the idea behind omnipolar
methods (m03) [@masse2016; @deno2017], was independent of direction at 0.2-mm spacing and varied by up to 20% at 2 mm
(lab part B). A simulation found modified omnipolar maps more accurate than bipolar maps at detecting fibrosis
[@riccio2021].

::: {.demo #m23-d1 badge="exact"}

```{=html}
<script type="module" src="../demos/m23-d1-direction.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: the m03 arctangent front, planar, crossing healthy tissue; peak-to-peak amplitudes computed exactly on the
  closed-form signals of one bipole and of two orthogonal bipoles sharing a center
  (@eq-m23-amplitude, @eq-m23-direction). Tested against `epml.voltage`.
- Parameters: front width 0.3 mm (m03); default height 1 mm [@riccio2021] and spacing 2 mm [@iafdb], as in m03; the
  default threshold 0.33 is the ratio of the 0.5-mV and 1.5-mV cutoffs [@marchlinski2000].
- What it ignores: directions out of the tissue plane, curved fronts, noise (@eq-m23-noise), heterogeneous tissue and
  electrode size.
:::

### Noise floor

With no local signal, the peak-to-peak of $n$ independent noise samples is still positive:

$$
\mathrm E[\operatorname{pp}] = 2\sigma\int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x\, n\,\phi(x)\,\Phi(x)^{n-1}\,dx
$$ {#eq-m23-noise}

That is about $3.1\sigma$ for 10 samples, $5.0\sigma$ for 100 and $6.5\sigma$ for 1000 (lab part C). With an
illustrative noise SD of 0.02 mV and 100 independent samples in the window, the floor is 0.10 mV: nothing below it
can be mapped. Filtering makes samples dependent, so $n$ is the number of independent samples, not of raw samples.

### Cutoffs

Model the voltages of scar and healthy tissue as log-normal. A cutoff $t$ then gives:

$$
\text{sensitivity} = \Phi\Bigl(\frac{\ln t - \ln m_s}{\sigma_s}\Bigr), \qquad \text{specificity} = 1 - \Phi\Bigl(\frac{\ln t - \ln m_n}{\sigma_n}\Bigr), \qquad t^* = \sqrt{m_s m_n} \text{ if } \sigma_s = \sigma_n
$$ {#eq-m23-threshold}

The last result maximizes sensitivity plus specificity. With illustrative medians of 0.2 and 2.5 mV and a log SD of
0.7, a 1.5-mV cutoff caught 99.8% of scar but called 23% of healthy tissue low. A 1-mm lift of a 2-mm bipole scaled
every reading by 0.42 and raised that to 70% (lab part D). Cutoffs found by ROC analysis against imaging depend on the
catheter, the chamber and contact: one study found 1.76 mV bipolar and 5.19 mV unipolar after excluding very low
contact force, with sensitivity and specificity of 0.90/0.90 and 0.89/0.85 [@teijeira2018].

::: {.demo #m23-d2 badge="approximate model"}
```{=html}
<div id="m23-d2-root" class="demo-root" data-demo="m23-d2"></div>
<script type="module" src="../demos/m23-d2-threshold.js"></script>
```

**Assumptions**

- Model: log-normal voltages for scar and healthy tissue with equal spread (@eq-m23-threshold); extra height scales
  every reading by the exact factor for an aligned 2-mm bipole (@eq-m23-amplitude). Tested against `epml.voltage`.
- Parameters: medians 0.2 and 2.5 mV and the spread are illustrative; the default cutoff 1.5 mV is the classic normal
  cutoff [@marchlinski2000]; base height 1 mm [@riccio2021].
- What it ignores: direction (@eq-m23-direction), noise (@eq-m23-noise), border-zone tissue between the two classes,
  and correlation between neighboring points.
:::

**Key takeaways**

- A cutoff is a choice of operating point, not a property of tissue.
- Poor contact shifts healthy tissue toward low voltage; direction does too.

## Clinical correlate

::: {.callout-note title="Pending clinical review"}
This section describes published findings only. It is not guidance for patient care, and it has
not yet been reviewed by an EP physician.
:::

**Where this shows up in EP.** Voltage maps are used to outline scar and diseased tissue. The classic ventricular
cutoffs came from a small series [@marchlinski2000]. Atrial normal values have been measured for different electrode
sizes [@anter2015]. Contact force [@teijeira2018] and activation direction, especially for a stationary catheter
[@yavin2021], change the voltage recorded from the same tissue.

**What the evidence is.** Clinical series [@marchlinski2000; @anter2015], a study against MRI [@teijeira2018], an
animal study [@yavin2021] and a simulation study [@riccio2021].

**What a reader should ask:**

- **Which catheter, spacing and electrode size?** (@eq-m23-amplitude)
- **Was contact controlled?** (@eq-m23-amplitude)
- **Were points collected from many directions or one?** (@eq-m23-direction)
- **What is the noise floor of the recording?** (@eq-m23-noise)
- **How were the cutoffs chosen, and against what reference?** (@eq-m23-threshold)

## How experts think

Before reading low voltage as scar, ask:

1. **Was the electrode in contact?** (@eq-m23-amplitude)
2. **Could the wavefront have run across the bipole?** (@eq-m23-direction)
3. **Is the amplitude above the noise floor?** (@eq-m23-noise)
4. **Which cutoff, for which catheter, validated against what?** (@eq-m23-threshold)
5. **Does the low-voltage region persist with another rhythm or direction?** (@eq-m23-direction)

One sentence to keep: **a voltage map measures tissue, contact, direction and noise together.**

## Cheat sheet

| Quantity | Result |
| --- | --- |
| Amplitude (@eq-m23-amplitude) | $\operatorname{pp}(U) = A/a$; $\operatorname{pp}(B) \to \tfrac98 A d\lvert\cos\theta\rvert/a^2$ (small $d$), $\to A/a$ (large $d$) |
| Direction (@eq-m23-direction) | $P(\lvert\cos\theta\rvert < q) = \tfrac2\pi\arcsin q$; pair $\ge 1/\sqrt2$ |
| Noise (@eq-m23-noise) | $\mathrm E[\operatorname{pp}] = 2\sigma\,\mathrm E[\max_n]$: about $5\sigma$ for 100 samples |
| Cutoffs (@eq-m23-threshold) | log-normal sensitivity and specificity; $t^* = \sqrt{m_s m_n}$ for equal spreads |

**Values used in this module**

| Value | Source |
| --- | --- |
| Normal > 1.5 mV, dense scar < 0.5 mV (ventricle) | @marchlinski2000 |
| Atrial fifth percentile 0.48 mV (3.5 mm) and 0.52 mV (1 mm); low-voltage area 20.4 vs 14.7 cm² | @anter2015 |
| Cutoffs 1.76 mV bipolar, 5.19 mV unipolar against MRI; 14 patients | @teijeira2018 |
| Orthogonal-direction difference 32% stationary, 11% roving; 10 swine | @yavin2021 |
| Height 1 mm; spacing 2 mm | @riccio2021, @iafdb |
| Tissue medians, spreads, noise SD, sample counts | illustrative |
| Amplitude ratios, direction fractions, noise floors, rates | our own code |

## Practice questions

Try each question before you open its model answer. In your answer, say which assumptions you
are making.

**Q1. What does a voltage map show?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The peak-to-peak amplitude of the electrogram at each site, unipolar or bipolar (@eq-m23-amplitude).

</details>

**Q2. Why does bipolar voltage depend more on contact than unipolar?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

A close bipole measures a spatial derivative, which falls as $1/a^2$, against $1/a$ for unipolar (@eq-m23-amplitude).

</details>

**Q3. Why can't you transfer a voltage cutoff between catheters?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Bipolar amplitude depends on spacing and electrode size (@eq-m23-amplitude); normal values have been measured per
catheter [@anter2015].

</details>

**Q4. A healthy site reads low on one bipole. What else could explain it?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The wavefront ran nearly perpendicular to the bipole, the electrode was not in contact, or the reading is at the noise
floor (@eq-m23-direction, @eq-m23-amplitude, @eq-m23-noise).

</details>

**Q5. Derive the fraction of random directions in which a bipole reads below a fraction q of its aligned value.**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

$\lvert\cos\theta\rvert < q$ on an interval of length $\pi - 2\arccos q$ out of $\pi$, so $\tfrac2\pi\arcsin
q$ (@eq-m23-direction).

</details>

**Q6. How do two orthogonal bipoles help?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Their larger amplitude is at least $1/\sqrt2$ of the aligned value; projecting the pair onto the best direction
recovers it at small spacing (@eq-m23-direction) [@masse2016].

</details>

**Q7. Does direction matter less for a roving catheter?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

In one animal study it did: 11% against 32% for a stationary array, because each site is sampled at several angles
[@yavin2021].

</details>

**Q8. What sets the lowest voltage a map can show?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

The peak-to-peak of noise in the measurement window, about five noise SDs for 100 independent
samples (@eq-m23-noise).

</details>

**Q9. How would you choose a cutoff?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

Against a reference such as imaging, with an ROC curve, choosing the operating point for the
purpose (@eq-m23-threshold) [@teijeira2018].

</details>

**Q10. Two log-normal populations with equal spread. Where does sensitivity plus specificity peak?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

At the geometric mean of the medians (@eq-m23-threshold).

</details>

**Q11. Where did the 0.5-mV and 1.5-mV ventricular cutoffs come from?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

1.5 mV from sinus-rhythm maps of 6 patients without structural heart disease; 0.5 mV was used for dense scar
[@marchlinski2000].

</details>

**Q12. Smaller electrodes found less low-voltage area in atrial scar. Why might that be?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Model answer</summary>

They average over less tissue and record more distinct local signals, so surviving muscle reads higher [@anter2015];
the m03 disk average shows the spatial filtering.

</details>

## Self-check

Short checks you can do in your head. Open each answer after you have tried it.

**S1. $a$ goes from 1 mm to 2 mm. Unipolar amplitude changes by what factor?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1/2 (@eq-m23-amplitude).

</details>

**S2. Same change, a very close bipole?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

1/4 (@eq-m23-amplitude).

</details>

**S3. A close bipole at 60° to propagation reads what fraction of its aligned amplitude?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\cos 60° =$ 0.5 (@eq-m23-direction).

</details>

**S4. Random directions; fraction reading below half of aligned?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\tfrac2\pi\arcsin 0.5 = 1/3$ (@eq-m23-direction).

</details>

**S5. Two independent unit-normal samples. Expected peak-to-peak?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$2/\sqrt\pi \approx$ 1.13 (@eq-m23-noise).

</details>

**S6. Medians 0.25 and 4 mV, equal spread. Best cutoff for sensitivity plus specificity?**

<details class="model-answer">
<summary>Answer</summary>

$\sqrt{0.25 \times 4} =$ 1 mV (@eq-m23-threshold).

</details>

## Literature figures

These figures are worth looking at alongside this module. We link to them instead of copying them:
some licenses do not allow reuse here, and others we could not confirm. Each entry says what to
look for and where this module explains it.

- **Voltage and electrode size.** Anter and colleagues' paired maps with large and small electrodes [@anter2015].
  This module: amplitude.
- **Direction in stationary and roving maps.** Yavin and colleagues' maps of one gap from four directions
  [@yavin2021]. This module: direction.
- **Voltage against MRI scar.** Teijeira-Fernandez and colleagues' ROC curves with and without contact-force
  filtering [@teijeira2018]. This module: cutoffs.

## Further reading

- **Cutoffs.** The classic ventricular values [@marchlinski2000]; atrial values by electrode size [@anter2015];
  validation against MRI [@teijeira2018].
- **Direction.** Animal data [@yavin2021]; omnipolar methods [@masse2016; @deno2017; @riccio2021].
- **Related modules.** m03 (electrograms), m13 (catheter design), m22 (annotation), m24 (interpolation), m26 (map
